title: The License to Depart
subtitle: Three last names, and how to say goodbye to a demon
blurb: The grimoire fills to seventy-two of seventy-two, the book circles back to its brass jar, and the Keeper shows you the most important page in it: the one about leaving.

segments.t: Last night I left you with a mirror. Tonight I owe you a door. Because every summoning in this book ends the same way. Not with a bang. Not with fire, or a scream, or a bargain signed in anything red. It ends with good manners. The magician thanks the spirit. And then, politely and firmly, he tells it to go home.

This is the twelfth night, and the last. Your grimoire has three empty places left in it. We are going to fill them, close the book the way it closes itself, and then I will walk you to the stairs. Bring the lamp. Three names.

The first has been waiting a long time. Number forty-three. Sabnock. A Marquis, mighty, great and strong, with fifty legions. He comes as an armed soldier with a lion's head, riding a pale horse. And his office is building. High towers, castles, whole cities, and he furnishes them with armour. He also gives good familiars, a familiar being a small attendant spirit that stays at your side. You have met builders on other nights. He is the last of them.

And because this book never gives with one hand only, the same entry says he afflicts men for many days with wounds and sores. He raises the walls and rots the men behind them. Anyone who has read about a siege will call that an accurate description of a fortress.

Now leave the walls behind. Number seventy. Seere. A mighty Prince, with twenty-six legions, and he appears as a beautiful man riding a winged horse. His office, the book says, is to go and come. That is nearly all. He carries things where you want them. He brings an abundance of things to pass on a sudden. And he is fast.
He can pass over the whole Earth in the twinkling of an Eye. He giveth a True relation of all sorts of Theft, and of Treasure hid, and of many other things.

He is of an indifferent good nature, the book adds, and willing to do anything the exorcist desires. The exorcist is simply the book's word for the magician. And indifferent does not mean he does not care. It is the old sense. Fairly. Tolerably good-natured. After sixty-nine entries of fire, flattery and worms, here is a spirit whose worst quality is being obliging. He may be the gentlest thing in these pages. He is practically a courier.

And then the last. Number seventy-two. Andromalius. An Earl, great and mighty, with thirty-six legions. He appears as a man holding a great serpent in his hand. No horse. No crown. No trumpets going before him. Just a man and a snake. He is the book's thief-taker, and its finder of hidden treasure. Listen.

His Office is to bring back both a Thief, and the Goods which be stolen; and to discover all Wickedness, and Underhand Dealing; and to punish all Thieves and other Wicked People and also to discover Treasures that be Hid.

A catalogue of seventy-two devils, and the very last one catches thieves. He returns what was taken. The list that opened with a king who makes you invisible closes with an earl who finds you out. Joke, warning, or accident, I cannot tell you. But the list ends on a demon of justice.

One honest footnote, since it is the last night. These final names are latecomers. When the doctor, Johann Weyer, printed his list of spirits in fifteen seventy-seven, Seere was not on it. Neither was Andromalius. They turn up in the English manuscripts of the following century, and nobody knows where the copyists found them. Somebody, quite late, decided the list needed an ending.

Now look at your grimoire. Go on. If you have kept every night, there is no blank left in it. Seventy-two of seventy-two. Every seal drawn. It took Solomon a ring and an angel. It took you twelve evenings and a little nerve.

threshold.q: Seventy-two faces, and you will not keep them all. Nobody does. So tell me. When the rest have faded, which one will you remember?

opts.label: The hoarse king
opts.reply: Bael. The first one through the door. People do remember the first, the way you remember the first step down into cold water. If you ever hear a cat, a toad and a man clear their throats at once, be civil. Tell him the Keeper sends her regards. He will know who you mean.

opts.label: The homesick phoenix
opts.reply: I hoped someone would say that. A bird with a child's voice, counting the centuries until it might be let back in. Of all of them, that is the one I would least like to forget. Keep it somewhere warm. Things that want to go home deserve to be remembered by somebody.

opts.label: The doctor, frankly
opts.reply: Weyer. Of course. The one name on the shelf that belonged to a living man, who copied out a list of demons to argue for mercy toward real people. You came for the evidence, and I respect it. He would have liked you. He would have asked for your sources first.

segments.t: Hold on to that one. Now watch what the book does when it runs out of names. It does not stop. Straight after Andromalius, without so much as a blank line, it tells a story. And it is a story you already know.
These be the seventy-two mighty Kings and Princes which King Solomon commanded into a Vessel of Brass, together with their Legions.

You heard that line on the first night. It was the first thing the book ever said to you. What I only mentioned in passing then is that it comes at the end of the list, not the beginning. The jar, the pride, the lake, the broken seal. The catalogue finishes by explaining why there is a catalogue. The snake has its tail in its mouth. We began where it ends.

And look who came out of that jar for you. A hoarse king who was a cat and a toad and a man all at once. A phoenix with a child's voice, hoping to go home. A duke with every face there is. And walking among them, entirely human, a doctor who printed the whole list while arguing that the women being burned as witches were innocent. History, as ever, is where the bodies are.

So. The names are said. In the book's imagination the spirit has come, and has answered every question. What now? This is the part the films leave out. The text is clear that whatever has been called must be sent. And the sending has a name. The License to Depart. It is the last thing the magician says to the spirit. He speaks its name, and then this.

Because thou hast diligently answered unto my demands, and hast been very ready and willing to come at my call, I do here license thee to depart unto thy proper place; without causing harm or danger unto man or beast.

Depart, then, I say, and be thou very ready to come at my call, being duly exorcised and conjured by the sacred rites of magic. I charge thee to withdraw peaceably and quietly, and the peace of God be ever continued between thee and me. Amen.

Listen to the temperature of that. After pages of threats, of chains and fire and terrible names, the last word to a demon is very nearly thank you. You answered. Go home, and hurt no one on the way, man or beast. And then the line I can never quite get past. The peace of God be ever continued between thee and me. Between a magician and a devil. Peace.

The book adds one more rule, and I report it as history, not as advice. The magician is not to leave his circle until the spirit has gone. That fear runs through the old stories. The apprentice who can start the thing and cannot stop it. The tales are almost never about the summoning. They are about the goodbye somebody forgot to say.

Which is why I think this is the most important page in a book about demons. Anyone can open a door. The rare skill is closing one. Saying, that is enough, and meaning it. Read the Lesser Key as psychology, as we did last night, and the License is the moment you put the dark thing down and it stays down. Read it as literature, and it is simply a good ending. Firm, courteous, and short.

threshold.q: Which means it is nearly time for yours. But first. You have spent twelve nights down here with me. What do you take with you up the stairs?

opts.label: The history
opts.reply: Then you leave heavier than you came, and better armed. Manuscripts, forgeries, a doctor, a sceptic, two quarrelling magicians. You know now that every demon has a paper trail. Follow it. And when you find the mistake I surely made somewhere in these twelve nights, be kind about it. Go well, scholar.

opts.label: The shiver
opts.reply: Good. Keep it. That small cold drop in the stomach is the oldest thing this book sells, and you paid for it honestly, by listening in the dark. It will fade by breakfast. It always does. But you will know where the stairs are if you ever want it back. Go well, seeker.

opts.label: Only the manners
opts.reply: Then you have taken the best thing in it. Not a name, not a seal. Just the idea that even the worst guest should be thanked, and shown out gently, and wished peace at the door. Most people leave here with a demon. You are leaving with a courtesy. Go well, poet.

segments.t: Then you still have a hand free, and I would like to put some books in it. If you want to keep reading, here is where a beginner should go next. No page numbers. Just a shelf.

For the Lesser Key itself, the scholarly edition by Joseph Peterson. He went back to the old handwritten copies and shows you where they disagree. For the bigger story, a history by Owen Davies, called simply Grimoires. It follows books of magic from the ancient world to the paperback rack, and it is better company than it has any right to be.

Then the old voices. The Testament of Solomon, where the ring and the interviews begin. It is short, strange, and free to read online. So are Johann Weyer and Reginald Scot, the two doubters who printed the list of spirits and, by printing it, preserved it. And for the pictures, the Dictionnaire Infernal, a French dictionary of demons whose illustrated edition gave these spirits the faces most people now imagine.

And one piece of advice, the same one I gave you last night. Read the sceptics and the believers side by side. The magician next to the historian. Each of them is right about something the other cannot see, and the truth about this book lives in the gap between their chairs. Anyone who offers you only one of them is selling something.

One more thing before the stairs. There is a page in your grimoire marked You. A confession. Every time I asked you a question on these nights, I kept a note of your answer. Scholar, seeker, sceptic, poet. It is all there. And on that page you can give it any word you like, your own name even, and it will draw you a seal of your own. It summons nothing. It is a keepsake. A pressed flower from a strange garden.

Now. Look up. There is grey light at the top of the stairs. It is always night down here, and I have rather lost the habit of mornings. But the lamp is paler than it was, and that means it is time. I know the form. So stand there a moment, and let me do this properly.

Listener. Because you have diligently attended to my stories, and have been very ready and willing to come at my call, twelve nights running, I do here license you to depart unto your proper place. Without harm or danger to man or beast. Go peaceably. Go quietly. And let there be peace, always, between you and me.

The seventy-two are in your grimoire, and they will keep. You know their names now. You know what each is said to do, who wrote it down, and who doubted. That is all a key ever was. Come back whenever you like. I will be here, holding the lamp. Mind the stairs on your way up. And for the first time in twelve nights, I get to say it. Good morning.

glossary.def: An attendant spirit said to serve a magician. Several spirits of the Goetia are described as giving good familiars.
In the Goetia, simply the magician: the person who calls and commands a spirit. The modern meaning, someone who drives a spirit out, came to dominate later.
The False Monarchy of Demons. A list of sixty-nine spirits that the physician Johann Weyer added to his book against witch-hunting in 1577. The main ancestor of the Goetia.
The formal dismissal that ends every working in the book: the spirit is thanked and told to return peaceably to its place, harming no one.
